## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your ability to design end-to-end provenance controls for CNF environments, specifically addressing how key rotation impacts SBOM generation and policy enforcement in multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters.

## Key Concepts
- Cosign image signing with KMS-backed keys
- SPDX SBOM generation and attestation workflows
- Kyverno policy enforcement for signature and SBOM validation
- Key rotation impact on image provenance chains
- Namespace-scoped testing strategies and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```bash
# Sign image with KMS-backed key
cosign sign --key kms://mykms/path/to/key \
  --attachment sbom \
  registry.example.com/cnf:latest

# Generate and attach SBOM
syft registry.example.com/cnf:latest \
  -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx

cosign attest --key kms://mykms/path/to/key \
  --type spdx --predicate sbom.spdx \
  registry.example.com/cnf:latest
```

## Implementation Strategy
Deploy this solution progressively: start with image signing, add SBOM generation, implement Kyverno policies, then automate the key rotation workflow. Test in isolated namespaces before cluster-wide deployment.

## Why This Is Asked
This tests ability to implement zero-downtime upgrades in a multi-tenant CNF gateway, focusing on per-tenant isolation, cross-namespace coordination, and robust failure handling.

## Key Concepts
- Graceful drain: per-tenant drain window, preStop, readiness gates
- Global upgrade control: ConfigMap flag
- Control-plane signaling: endpoint or event
- Failure modes: stuck drains, failed signal, burst load

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf-upgrade
  namespace: tenant-a
data:
  upgradePause: "true"
```

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: gateway-tenant-a
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: cnf/gateway:latest
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:9000/drain || true"]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 9000
              protocol: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the drain behavior under bursty traffic?
- How would you handle tenants with long-lived streams (WebSockets)?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical cache design in a CNF gateway, focusing on tenant isolation, hot-path optimization, and lifecycle of cached data.

## Key Concepts
- Cache-aside pattern with per-tenant keys
- Redis TTL and path-based keys
- ConfigMap-driven hot-paths per tenant
- Background refresh to avoid stale data

## Code Example
```go
package main

import (
  "time"
  "context"
  "github.com/go-redis/redis/v8"
)

type CacheClient struct{ Redis *redis.Client }

func (c *CacheClient) Get(ctx context.Context, tenant, path string) ([]byte, error) {
  key := tenant + ":" + path
  val, err := c.Redis.Get(ctx, key).Bytes()
  if err == nil {
    return val, nil
  }
  resp := fetchFromBackend(path) // placeholder
  c.Redis.Set(ctx, key, resp, 30*time.Second)
  return resp, nil
}
```
